frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons while using gas exports to preserve leverage with Europe. Aging fields, investment needs, and European diversification efforts limit that leverage over time.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in construction, transport, and energy infrastructure. Algiers generally keeps financing and strategic assets under national oversight, limiting direct external control.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Backed Financial Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola has reduced some opaque oil-backed arrangements but remains highly dependent on hydrocarbons and external capital. Debt service and production decline constrain Luanda's ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is drawing strong Western and regional interest as a route for critical minerals from the Copperbelt. Infrastructure investment can diversify Angola's economy, but foreign operators and financiers will compete for long-term control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou is central to Benin's trade and regional influence, but its performance depends on cross-border access and external logistics investment. Competition with Lomé and shifting Niger relations expose the corridor to political disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Security Frontier
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity in the northern borderlands threatens roads, agricultural zones, and mining prospects. Benin is expanding security cooperation, but reliance on foreign equipment and intelligence remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains unusually strong institutions and bargaining power over diamond revenues, but its fiscal model remains exposed to global diamond demand and synthetic-stone competition. The state is seeking greater downstream value and economic diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are showing increased interest in Botswana's copper, nickel, and other mineral prospects. Gaborone has room to negotiate favorable terms, although limited infrastructure and market scale constrain options.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing greater state participation and tighter oversight of gold production, including pressure on foreign mining interests. Informal extraction, smuggling, and weak administrative reach continue to reduce sovereign capture.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou has deepened security ties with Russia while reducing reliance on France and other Western partners. This may reinforce political autonomy, but opaque security arrangements and persistent insurgency risk increasing external leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-earth mining remain vulnerable to opaque licensing, smuggling, and limited state oversight. The government is seeking greater formal control, but bargaining power and enforcement capacity remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed-group activity in eastern DRC and alleged cross-border support. This constrains trade and diverts resources toward security rather than infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and maritime-security development relies heavily on foreign financing and partnerships, including European, American, and Chinese-linked actors. This expands connectivity while limiting full sovereign control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Water Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, desalination, and tourism revenue leaves the islands exposed to shipping disruptions and climate stress. Renewable-energy expansion is improving resilience but remains insufficient for full strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Backed Resource Corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Kribi port, rail, mining, and timber corridors are increasingly tied to foreign capital, especially Chinese and Gulf-linked commercial interests. Cameroon retains formal ownership, but debt, concession, and security arrangements constrain effective control.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Infrastructure Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest continues to damage roads, plantations, schools, and local commerce. The conflict also raises operating costs for strategic transport and agricultural supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and affiliated commercial networks remain closely associated with regime protection and access to gold and diamond concessions. This strengthens short-term state survival while reducing transparency and local capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Peripheral Armed-Group Control
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups continue to contest territory and transport routes outside major government-held centers. Weak roads and insecure mining zones prevent Bangui from exercising consistent sovereignty over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports through the Chad-Cameroon pipeline remain central to state finances and expose N'Djamena to foreign operators, transit infrastructure, and price volatility. Revenue concentration limits diversification and weakens broad-based domestic control of the economy.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Balancing
frictionVectors.details: Chad is recalibrating ties among France, the United States, Russia-linked actors, and regional partners while facing instability spilling from Sudan and the wider Sahel. Foreign security relationships provide leverage but can constrain independent strategic decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: France–Mayotte Sovereignty Tension
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved status of Mayotte continues to limit diplomatic normalization with France, while migration and maritime-security issues keep the dispute politically active.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external financing and diaspora remittances for transport, energy, and public investment, constraining independent control over development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt supply chains remain dominated by foreign capital, processing capacity, and trading networks, limiting Kinshasa's ability to capture full value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict Corridors and Foreign Backing
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity and regional rivalries continue to threaten mining zones and transport routes, enabling external actors to shape security and resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the core source of export earnings and fiscal strength, leaving national resource control vulnerable to production declines, opaque contracting, and external energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and financing have expanded infrastructure, but debt obligations and project terms can narrow the government's room to set independent investment priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cocoa Chain
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is strengthening local processing and regulatory capacity, but foreign traders and manufacturers still capture substantial value beyond the farm gate.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability from Burkina Faso and Mali continues to pressure northern border infrastructure, trade routes, and security spending while increasing dependence on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Multiple foreign military facilities provide revenue and diplomatic leverage, but their concentration also limits Djibouti's strategic autonomy and exposes it to great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and associated debt ties, particularly involving Chinese financing and regional trade, give external actors substantial influence over the country's economic strategy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating agreement for the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The dispute remains tied to wider Red Sea and Gulf competition.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs and major Gulf investments provide essential liquidity but increase outside influence over strategic assets, currency policy, and infrastructure priorities.

highlights: China remains a key infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling legacy production is tightening government revenues and increasing pressure to attract foreign operators under less favorable bargaining conditions. Gas monetization and offshore development remain central to preserving state control.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a major role in ports, roads, and public construction, creating financing and debt-linked leverage over strategic infrastructure despite the government's preference for centralized control.

highlights: Red Sea access raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide scarce foreign exchange but rely heavily on external capital and technical capacity. Opaque contracting and limited transparency constrain domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to Yemen make its ports strategically valuable to Gulf and wider external powers. This creates opportunities for revenue and leverage but also exposes sovereignty to security bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: South African dependency
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South Africa for trade routes, electricity, logistics, and market access. This limits independent infrastructure and resource-policy choices even without direct political control.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and investment concentration
frictionVectors.details: The sugar sector and export-processing industries remain vulnerable to external market rules and concentrated foreign ownership. Efforts to diversify into manufacturing and logistics have produced limited sovereign capacity gains.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy and power exports
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's control over electricity generation and potential exports but continues to provoke Egyptian and Sudanese security concerns. Disputes over filling, drought management, and data sharing remain unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, Chinese-linked infrastructure, Gulf investment, and foreign currency shortages limit Addis Ababa's room to set infrastructure priorities independently. Conflict-related instability further weakens bargaining power over transport, telecom, and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater state participation and domestic processing in manganese and other minerals, but remains dependent on foreign capital, technology, and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Transition-Era Governance Risk
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo political order has strengthened executive control, yet uncertainty over institutional checks and contract continuity could complicate long-term resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on external financing and regional arrangements, particularly with Senegal, to sustain port access, transport links, and energy security.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited monitoring capacity constrain the government's ability to secure coastal resources and capture their full economic value.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining Crisis
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and environmentally destructive gold mining erodes state authority, damages water systems, and creates persistent tensions involving domestic operators and foreign-linked networks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and fiscal pressure limit Accra's ability to finance infrastructure and negotiate from strength with mining, petroleum, and energy investors.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign-Control Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project could transform national revenues, but its rail, port, and financing architecture leaves Guinea reliant on powerful external consortiums and Chinese-linked infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and Contract Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Military rule has increased state demands on mining firms while weakening transparent oversight, raising risks of abrupt contract revisions, elite capture, and investor-driven extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fisheries Access
frictionVectors.details: Limited maritime enforcement and fiscal dependence weaken Guinea-Bissau's ability to control its waters and secure fair returns from foreign fishing agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Narcotics and Political Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Institutional instability and transnational trafficking networks undermine sovereignty, divert state capacity, and increase the influence of external security and political actors.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and reliance on foreign-financed transport and energy projects constrain Nairobi's policy space. Public scrutiny is intensifying over concession terms, procurement transparency, and strategic asset control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa's role as a regional gateway faces competition from ports in Tanzania and Somaliland. Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests are competing for influence over logistics corridors serving East Africa.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa generate vital revenue but deepen structural dependence on Pretoria and expose Lesotho to disputes over pricing, construction delays, and project governance.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Mining Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to externally controlled textile supply chains and foreign-owned mining operations. Shifts in trade preferences or commodity prices can quickly reduce domestic employment and fiscal space.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Resource Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining projects dominate Liberia's export outlook, while transport, rail, and port arrangements determine how much value remains in-country. Concession renegotiation and local-content enforcement remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Control and modernization of the port are strategically important for customs revenue and regional trade. External operators and lenders can shape tariff policy, infrastructure priorities, and Liberia's commercial autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest authority over oil revenues, export terminals, and national institutions. Foreign states and energy firms retain leverage through security partnerships, market access, and technical operations.

frictionVectors.title: Militia-Controlled Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Production and exports remain vulnerable to blockades, sabotage, and bargaining by armed groups linked to local and foreign patrons. This fragments state authority and prevents durable national control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Large-Scale Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are heavily dependent on foreign capital and external markets. Fiscal benefits and local processing remain limited relative to the scale of environmental and infrastructure impacts.

frictionVectors.title: Land, Forest, and Maritime Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Illegal logging, land concessions, and competition over ports and maritime resources challenge Madagascar's control over its natural assets. External conservation, mining, and infrastructure actors often operate amid weak enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: IMF AND CREDITOR LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms limit fiscal room and influence decisions on subsidies, state enterprises, and infrastructure spending.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MINING CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Renewed uranium and critical-mineral investment could improve export earnings, but weak domestic financing and regulatory capacity leave Malawi exposed to unequal concessions.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD-SECTOR RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state participation and revenue shares, raising tensions with major international operators.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support expands Bamako's room to resist Western pressure but creates new external leverage and reputational risks around mining access.

frictionVectors.title: GREATER TORTUE AHMEYIM DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal offers new revenues, but foreign operators, shared-field governance, and export infrastructure limit Mauritania's near-term control.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE LOGISTICS BOTTLENECK
frictionVectors.details: State-backed rail and port infrastructure remains central to mineral exports, leaving the economy vulnerable to external finance, shipping conditions, and commodity-price swings.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS IMPLEMENTATION RISKS
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim has gained diplomatic ground, but the future of the Diego Garcia military facility and the terms of any long-term arrangement remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN PORT INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, British, and US strategic interests around maritime infrastructure create pressure for Mauritius to balance security partnerships without surrendering policy autonomy.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the strategic core

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Control and development of Western Sahara underpin Morocco's sovereignty strategy, while legal challenges and rival Algerian-backed claims complicate foreign investment.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Major renewable, port, rail, and industrial projects rely on European, Gulf, Chinese, and US capital, creating exposure to partner conditions despite strong Moroccan state coordination.

highlights: Ports and Gas Corridors Draw External Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed security support remains central to protecting LNG investments and transport corridors. Persistent insurgent attacks limit Maputo's ability to exercise uncontested authority over the gas-producing north.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Revenue and Contract Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies retain significant bargaining power over project timing, financing, and revenue structures. Delays and security costs continue to constrain the fiscal benefits available to the state.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Race Accelerates

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have attracted major foreign energy firms and raised expectations of rapid development. Namibia is seeking stronger local-content and fiscal safeguards before large-scale production begins.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects rely on foreign capital, technology, export markets, and transmission infrastructure. This creates a risk that Namibia captures fewer industrial benefits than headline investment figures suggest.

highlights: Junta Reclaims Uranium and Oil Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Contract Reset
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are renegotiating or restricting foreign access to strategic minerals, especially uranium, while seeking partners less politically conditional than France and Western firms. This may increase sovereign control but risks reduced investment and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Access Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Political ruptures with regional organizations and neighboring states complicate export routes, including oil infrastructure toward the Gulf of Guinea. Sanctions, insecurity, and reliance on external security partners remain major constraints.

highlights: China and Gulf Capital Expand Infrastructure Footprint

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Investment and Revenue Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Production reforms are attracting new investment, but crude theft, pipeline sabotage, and opaque contracting continue to weaken public control of petroleum value chains. Foreign operators and domestic intermediaries retain substantial leverage over project economics.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign financiers are expanding roles in rail, ports, and energy infrastructure. These deals can close critical gaps quickly but may create long-term repayment, concession, and sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Mineral Diplomacy Collides with DRC War

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral and Security Network
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces sustained international scrutiny over alleged support for M23 and the movement of minerals through eastern Congo, while Kigali denies or disputes key accusations. Sanctions and diplomatic pressure threaten trade access and external partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Strategic Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security and development model remains supported by foreign aid, investment, and security cooperation. Pressure over human rights and regional conduct could narrow Kigali's room to maneuver despite its strong administrative control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons attract foreign operators and political expectations, while limited state capacity constrains São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power. Unproven reserves and licensing uncertainty make near-term fiscal gains unlikely.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country remains reliant on external partners for infrastructure, budget support, and maritime security. Competition among Portuguese, Chinese, European, and Gulf-linked interests can narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas revenues offer Dakar greater fiscal leverage, but contract reviews and local-content demands risk friction with international operators and lenders. Managing transparency and revenue distribution will determine whether resource control materially improves.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's port, rail, and industrial corridors remain exposed to competition from regional hubs and foreign infrastructure finance. Dependence on external capital creates recurring tension between rapid development and strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from cooperation with India, France, the United States, and other partners for maritime surveillance and anti-piracy operations. This improves security but requires careful balancing among competing Indian Ocean powers.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and External Access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and tuna value chains remain central to the economy, creating leverage for outside actors. The government's ability to enforce sustainable quotas and capture more processing value is constrained by limited scale.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects attract foreign capital while exposing the state to commodity cycles, tax disputes, and environmental pressures. Stronger domestic processing and contract enforcement are needed to convert extraction into durable sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Queen Elizabeth II Quay
frictionVectors.details: Freetown's port expansion and logistics development are strategically important but rely heavily on foreign finance and operators. Infrastructure gains could improve trade while also creating long-term exposure to external commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Competition
frictionVectors.details: Federal authorities are pursuing offshore petroleum opportunities, but disagreements with member states and weak regulatory capacity complicate licensing and revenue sharing. Foreign operators and regional powers can exploit these institutional divisions.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Architecture
frictionVectors.details: Somalia depends on international and regional partners for counterinsurgency, maritime security, training, and infrastructure support. Turkish, Gulf, Western, and African involvement strengthens state capacity but limits independent control over strategic assets and security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mining ownership and beneficiation
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing and value capture from platinum-group metals, manganese and other minerals while managing investment concerns from multinational firms and strategic partners.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and constrained rail and port capacity continue to weaken sovereign control over export chains, increasing dependence on private operators and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on Sudanese pipelines and Port Sudan for oil exports, leaving revenues and production exposed to conflict, transit fees and external political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Armed competition over resources
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and localized armed violence constrain state control over oil regions, land and cross-border trade while foreign firms retain a central role in the energy sector.

highlights: Gold and ports draw external competition

frictionVectors.title: Gold networks and wartime finance
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain important sources of leverage for armed actors and external patrons, weakening civilian oversight and formal state revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated maritime infrastructure are strategically contested amid regional competition, while conflict has made export routes, humanitarian access and energy logistics highly vulnerable.

highlights: LNG and corridor projects reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and local content
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for stronger fiscal returns, domestic participation and safeguards in developing its offshore gas sector, but major projects remain dependent on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and strategic corridors
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades around Dar es Salaam and new transport corridors could expand sovereign leverage over regional trade, while concession terms and external financing remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Togo's maritime economy relies on foreign investment, shipping networks and external infrastructure finance, creating exposure to changing Gulf, Chinese and European commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate value capture
frictionVectors.details: The state retains strategic importance in phosphate production but faces pressure to improve processing, logistics and revenue capture rather than relying primarily on raw-material exports.

frictionVectors.title: European Leverage Over Migration and Finance
frictionVectors.details: EU funding and cooperation on migration remain politically important, increasing external influence over Tunisia's border and domestic policy choices. IMF-linked financing remains difficult amid resistance to austerity and state-enterprise reform.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported energy exposes Tunisia to fiscal and strategic pressure, while delayed renewable and interconnection projects limit near-term sovereignty gains.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Environmental Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces Western political pressure, financing constraints, and land and environmental disputes. Chinese and regional backing help offset reduced Western participation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Funded Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy infrastructure strengthens state capacity but increases repayment exposure and dependence on external contractors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is regaining leverage through mining-sector reforms and renewed investment, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and processing. Volatile copper prices remain a major constraint on sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Creditors
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has reduced immediate pressure, yet negotiations with bilateral and private creditors continue to shape fiscal and infrastructure policy. Chinese and Western partners remain influential in strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked firms remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and other mining projects, while Harare uses export restrictions and local-processing demands to capture more value. Limited domestic capital and technology constrain the government's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, Finance, and Infrastructure Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and restricted access to international finance raise infrastructure costs and push Zimbabwe toward narrower external partnerships. Power shortages and unreliable transport further reduce sovereign control over mineral supply chains.
